+| **Season** | a handful of dated performances, times vary | EIF theatre/opera/dance | high |
+| **One-off** | happens exactly once | Book Festival author events, most EIFF screenings, Jazz concerts | total |
+| **Anchor** | same show nightly, one venue, sold months ahead | the Tattoo | it's a commitment, not a candidate |
+| **Drop-in** | no start time — opening hours, you choose the duration | Art Festival exhibitions | none |
+| **Occasion** | one dated outdoor thing, no seat, no slot | the Carnival parade, Meadows Festival, Folk & Food | total |
+
+Only **Run** is modelled today. **One-off** and **Drop-in** break the most
+assumptions: a one-off is a *point*, not a lane, and a drop-in has no start time
+to be reachable in time for.
+
+### The rule that keeps the two from fighting
+
+> **Shape decides the silhouette and the logic. Festival decides the colour and
+> the mark.**
+
+A Book Festival one-off and an EIFF one-off share a card shape — a dated point
+with a "once only" marker — but carry different festival colours. A Fringe run
+and an EIF season share a festival-agnostic time-block silhouette but differ in
+how many dates they offer. A drop-in exhibition looks like neither, in any
+festival's colours.
+
+This is what stops the design collapsing into either failure mode: eight
+identically-shaped cards in eight paint jobs (pretty, still lies about what the
+events *are*), or one shape per festival (breaks the moment a festival programmes
+something unusual — and they all do; EIF runs exhibitions, the Fringe runs
+free non-ticketed shows).
+
+### On festival branding, concretely
+
+Use the festival's **name and one colour token** per festival, plus a small
+geometric mark that is *ours*, not theirs. Do **not** reproduce festival logos or
+wordmarks — they are trademarks, and an unofficial aggregator reproducing eight
+of them invites a takedown that costs more than the design gains. This should be
+checked before shipping, not after.
+
+## 3. The Now page
+
+The Now page's soul is reachability, and that survives intact. Four changes, in
+descending order of value:
+
+### 3.1 The scarcity line (the highest-value addition)
+
+Every row gains one short phrase next to the reachability verdict:
+
+```
+21:15   "Be Good!" with Paulette          🚶 6 min · Free
+        Comedy · Underbelly               on again tomorrow
+
+19:30   Ali Smith: Changing Your Mind     🚶 11 min · £14
+        Book Festival · Futures Institute ⚡ only tonight
+```
+
+This is genuinely new information the Fringe-only product never needed — with one
+festival, everything repeats, so scarcity carries no signal. With eight, it is
+the difference between a casual choice and one worth rearranging an evening for.
+It is derived, not fetched: count the event's remaining performances.
+
+### 3.2 The drop-in answer to an empty list
+
+Today, when nothing fits, the page says *"Nothing reachable in the next couple of
+hours — widen your travel window or taste."* With the Art Festival present, the
+honest answer is usually better:
+
+> **Nothing starts in your window** — but 3 exhibitions near you are open now,
+> and you can leave whenever you like.
+
+A drop-in has no start time, so it can *never* fail the reachability test on
+timing — only on distance. It is the perfect filler for exactly the gap the Now
+page exists to serve, and it turns the product's worst state into a useful one.
+Drop-ins should be a distinct band below the timed list, not interleaved: they
+answer a different question and sorting them by start time is meaningless.
+
+### 3.3 A festival filter card, and a deliberate anti-Fringe bias
+
+A festival multi-select joins genre / subgenre / price / travel as a constraint
+card, following the existing pattern (live per-option counts, "everything!"
+reset). Default: all on.
+
+More interesting is the **ordering**. The stated goal is that users come away
+understanding Edinburgh's festival diversity — not merely that they extract
+maximum value. Those are different objectives and they conflict, because pure
+proximity ranking returns a Fringe-only list ~80% of the time.
+
+**Proposal: cap consecutive same-festival rows.** Within each start-time group,
+after N rows from one festival (N = 3 feels right), promote the next-best row
+from a different festival. The cost is honest and should be stated in the UI copy
+rather than hidden: occasionally a slightly further-away event appears above a
+closer one.
+
+This is a product-values decision, not an algorithm detail. It should be made
+explicitly by a human, and it is the single place in this proposal where the
+product deliberately gives up a little optimality to serve the "show them the
+city" goal. It is also trivially reversible — one constant.
+
+### 3.4 Ticket honesty across sources
+
+The Fringe scraper gives per-performance `ticketStatus`; the cross-festival data
+source has **no availability field at all** (§5). So the Fringe keeps its live
+`Sold out!` stamp and other festivals cannot have one.
+
+Do not paper over this. Non-Fringe rows carry no availability stamp and their
+action reads *"Check tickets ↗"* rather than *"Book"*. Inventing parity here
+would break the one thing the product brief insists on — *stale or wrong
+reachability is worse than no app* — and availability is the same promise.
+
+### 3.5 What deliberately does *not* change
+
+The constraint cards, the reachability calculation, the map, the journey strip.
+An event with a start time, a duration and coordinates flows through the existing
+engine unchanged regardless of which festival issued it. That is the whole reason
+this is tractable.
+
+## 4. The planner
+
+Correctly predicted to be the more intricate side, and it carries more value —
+because scarcity is a *planning* concept. Live, you can only catch what is on
+now; planning is where "this happens once, on the 19th" actually changes a
+decision.
+
+### 4.1 The grid's core assumption breaks
+
+Today: one lane per show, marks across Aug 1–31, scrub a date window. That is
+exactly right for a **Run** — the lane's density *is* the information.
+
+A **One-off** in that grid is a lane with a single mark and 30 empty cells. Fill
+a board with Book Festival events and the grid becomes a diagonal of dots: a lot
+of pixels saying very little, and worse, it looks like a show with terrible
+availability rather than a fixed point in time.
+
+**Proposal: two bands on one shared date axis.**
+
+```
+  ┌ FIXED POINTS ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
+  │ ●Book        ●Film    ●Film ●Jazz          ●Book          │   ← one-offs & occasions,
+  │      ▲Tattoo ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲            │      packed, not one per lane
+  ├ RUNS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
+  │ Paulette      ▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪                   │   ← lanes, exactly as today
+  │ Some Theatre    ▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪▪                            │
+  │ EIF Macbeth        ▪   ▪   ▪                              │
+  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
+       │◄──────── date window ────────►│
+```
+
+Same axis, same scrub, same window. One-offs are constraints on the window; runs
+are choices within it. Drawing them in the same visual language misrepresents
+both.
+
+### 4.2 Anchors go in first (an engine change)
+
+`buildSchedule`'s earliest-finish-first greedy assumes candidates are fungible —
+correct when every show has 25 chances. A one-off, a Tattoo ticket, or an EIF
+opening night is not a candidate the greedy may drop; it is a fixed point the
+rest of the day must accommodate.
+
+The seam already exists: **forced/pinned shows**. Pins already survive the
+per-day cap and the min-per-day drop, and a performance-level pin already
+overrides the day window and meal breaks. A one-off is, structurally, an
+**auto-pin** — the user selected the event, and the event selected its own date.
+
+So the change is smaller than it looks: seed the schedule with the shape-derived
+anchors, then run the existing greedy over the remaining runs. What genuinely
+needs new work is the **diagnostics** — `placementDiagnostics` currently
+attributes an unplaceable show to the control that would rescue it, and needs a
+new verdict for *"two one-offs collide and no control can fix it — one has to
+go."* That is a real user decision, and surfacing it well is most of the value.
+
+### 4.3 Scarcity-weighted "Pick my best dates" (the biggest unlock)
+
+Today the control scores each candidate window by how many favourites it catches.
+Every favourite counts 1. With one festival that is fine — everything repeats, so
+the score is essentially "how much of the run does this window overlap".
+
+With eight festivals it is actively wrong. A window catching three one-offs is
+worth far more than one catching three Fringe runs you could see on any other
+day, yet they score identically.
+
+**Proposal: weight each catchable event by its scarcity.**
+
+```
+weight(event) = 1 / (number of performances in the whole festival run)
+
+  one-off (1 performance)      → 1.00
+  EIF season (3 performances)  → 0.33
+  Fringe run (25 performances) → 0.04
+```
+
+Sum the weights over the window instead of counting. The effect is that "pick my
+best dates" stops being *"the week with the most stuff"* and becomes *"the week
+where the things you cannot otherwise see are happening"* — which is what a
+visitor choosing dates is actually asking. It is a handful of lines in the
+scoring pass and it changes the answer completely.
+
+Suggested UI honesty: show both numbers — *"catches 14 of your 18 — including 4
+you can only see this week."* The second clause is the one that decides a trip.
+
+### 4.4 Diversity as a stated plan property
+
+Per the goal that users should come away understanding the city's festival
+range, the plan panel should **report** diversity, not only volume:
+
+> **9 events across 5 festivals, in 4 days**
+
+Reporting is the safe version and should ship first. A **soft objective** —
+preferring a plan that touches one more festival over one that packs one more
+Fringe show — is the ambitious version, and it deserves its own decision because
+it means the planner sometimes returns fewer events on purpose. Worth noting that
+the widely-repeated Fringe advice already argues against pure maximisation
+("don't fill the day"; the rule of thirds), so this is less heretical than it
+sounds.
+
+If it ships, it should be a visible dial (*pack my days ⟷ show me the city*),
+never a hidden heuristic. A planner that silently drops a show the user selected,
+for a reason they cannot see, has broken its contract.
+
+### 4.5 Drop-ins are offered, never scheduled
+
+An exhibition must never be allocated a block by the greedy — it has no start
+time, so any block the scheduler invents is fiction.
+
+Instead, once the plan is built, walk its **gaps**: for each gap over ~45
+minutes, offer what is open then, near the venues on either side. This reuses the
+travel machinery unchanged and gives leftover time real value without pretending
+to schedule it.
+
+```
+  14:00  Some Theatre Show        Pleasance Dome
+         ↓ 1h50 gap · 6 min walk
+         ◇ 3 exhibitions open near here — all free, drop in
+  16:30  Ali Smith                Futures Institute
+```
+
+### 4.6 Travel gets a mode it does not have
+
+Venues spread well past the Old Town: Leith Theatre is a genuine 30+ minute walk,
+Church Hill Theatre is ~25 minutes south, and **Fringe by the Sea is ~25 miles
+away in North Berwick** — a train journey, not a walk. The haversine-plus-speed
+estimate is wrong by an order of magnitude there.
+
+The honest minimum is to mark out-of-city venues explicitly and refuse to
+estimate, rather than quietly returning a plausible-looking number. A "day trip"
+mode is a larger piece of work and probably should not gate the rest.
+
+### 4.7 Exports
+
+CSV and ICS both need `festival` and `shape` columns. A drop-in offer should
+probably not emit a timed calendar event at all — an all-day note, or nothing.
+
+## 5. Data
+
+### 5.1 The source exists and it is official
+
+`api.edinburghfestivalcity.com` — the **Edinburgh Festivals Listings API**, run
+by Festivals Edinburgh Limited, free with a registered key, covering all 11 major
+festivals (`festival` accepts `fringe, jazz, book, international, tattoo, art,
+hogmanay, science, imaginate, film, mela, storytelling`). 2026 data is loaded for
+every August festival.
+
+It carries what the product needs: venue `latitude`/`longitude`, a
+`performances[]` array of `{start, end, duration_minutes, price, concession,
+price_string, is_at_fixed_time}`, `genre`/`genre_tags`, images, wheelchair
+access, and `modified_from` for incremental sync.
+
+Two findings worth calling out:
+
+- **`is_at_fixed_time` is the drop-in flag.** The API already separates a timed
+  performance from an open-hours one — the exact distinction §2 needs, provided
+  for free.
+- **It carries real prices.** The edfringe GraphQL API deliberately does not
+  (only `priceType` flags), and the product brief currently apologises for that
+  limitation. This would close it for seven of the eight festivals.
+
+### 5.2 The blocker: licence versus this repo's architecture
+
+Commercial use is explicitly permitted and attribution is required (a visible
+credit and a link). But developer users **must not redistribute listings to third
+parties by means of data feeds or data dumps**, and applications must refresh at
+least every 24 hours.
+
+This repo **commits its normalized catalogue to a public git repository and
+serves it as a static JSON file from GitHub Pages**. Whether that reads as
+"serving your own app's users" (clearly the intended pattern — the whole project
+gallery works this way) or as "redistributing a data dump" is not something to
+infer from a terms page. **Ask Festivals Edinburgh directly before building on
+it.** This is the one genuine blocker in the proposal, and it is cheap to
+resolve: one email.
+
+Fallbacks if the answer is no: fetch client-side per user (but then the key is
+public), or serve only a reduced derivative and link out for detail.
+
+### 5.3 Keep the Fringe on its own scraper
+
+The existing edfringe GraphQL scraper stays the better Fringe source:
+per-performance `ticketStatus`, the 104-label subgenre taxonomy, content warnings
+and age guidance, all at a fidelity the Listings API does not match. Two adapters
+into one normalized schema — not a migration.
+
+### 5.4 Schema additions
+
+```jsonc
+{
+  "festival":  "book",              // festival key — drives colour, mark, filter
+  "shape":     "one-off",           // run | season | one-off | anchor | drop-in | occasion
+  "chances":   1,                   // performances in the whole run — drives scarcity
+  "ticketing": "external",          // live | external | none  (§3.4 honesty)
+  "outOfCity": false,               // suppresses walk estimates (§4.6)
+  "openHours": null                 // { open, close } for drop-in shapes
+}
+```
+
+`shape` is **derived at normalize time**, not fetched: `is_at_fixed_time` false →
+`drop-in`; then bucket on performance count and cadence (1 → `one-off`, 2–6 →
+`season`, near-daily long run → `run`, and the Tattoo is a hand-set `anchor`).
+Deriving it in the pipeline rather than the client keeps both front ends and the
+engine free of festival-specific special cases — which is the property that makes
+the ninth festival cheap to add.
+
+## 6. What this costs
+
+Stated plainly, because each is a real trade:
+
+- **The name.** "EdFringeNow", covering eight festivals, is a mismatch. Not for
+  this document to decide, but it will be asked the moment this ships.
+- **Fringe depth versus city breadth.** Effort spent on cross-festival shape
+  handling is effort not spent on the Fringe's live-reachability edge, which is
+  still the product's most distinct claim and still unmatched by competitors.
+- **The availability asymmetry is permanent** until another source appears. Users
+  will notice that some events say "sold out" and others say nothing.
+- **A second data dependency**, on a licence we do not control and a refresh
+  cadence we must honour.
+- **Diversity ranking gives up optimality on purpose.** Defensible, but it must
+  be a stated value, visible in the UI, not a silent thumb on the scale.
+
+## 7. Phasing
+
+| Phase | What | Gate |
+|---|---|---|
+| **0** | Email Festivals Edinburgh about the static-file question; register a key; make one real call | Blocks everything |
+| **1** | Schema + adapter. Fringe only, everything `shape: "run"`. **No visible change** | The refactor is provably inert |
+| **2** | Now page: festival filter, festival marks, scarcity line, drop-in empty state | The cheapest real user value |
+| **3** | Planner: two-band grid, anchors, scarcity-weighted best dates, gap offers | The intricate part |
+| **4** | Diversity reporting; the pack ⟷ explore dial if wanted | Values decision first |
+
+Phase 1 is the one worth insisting on: shipping the schema change with no user-visible
+effect is what proves the abstraction holds before any of it is load-bearing.
+
+## 8. Decisions this proposal cannot make
+
+1. **Does the licence permit our architecture?** (§5.2 — blocks phase 1.)
+2. **Should ranking deliberately favour festival diversity over proximity?**
+   (§3.3 — a product-values call.)
+3. **Should the planner ever return fewer events to return more festivals?**
+   (§4.4 — the stronger version of the same call.)
+4. **Fringe depth or city breadth**, if the two compete for the next quarter.
+5. **The name**, eventually.
+
+## Sources
+
+- [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/) — [events fields](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/events), [venues fields](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/venues), [licence](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/licence), [2026 status](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/status), [projects](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/projects)
+- [Edinburgh Festivals: What's On in 2026](https://www.edinburghfestivalcity.com/inspiration/573-edinburgh-festivals-whats-on-in-2026)
+- [Edinburgh Festival 2026 dates (Data Thistle)](https://edinburghfestival.datathistle.com/festivals/)
+- [Edinburgh International Festival 2026](https://www.eif.co.uk/brochure)
+- [Book Festival 2026 programme — ~600 events, 41 countries](https://www.whatsoninedinburgh.co.uk/news/2026/06/16/nearly-600-writers-from-41-countries-to-gather-as-edinburgh-international-book-festival-returns-with-global-2026-programme/)
+- [Film Festival 2026 programme (Screen Scotland)](https://www.screen.scot/news/2026/july/edinburgh-international-film-festival-announces-2026-programme)
+- [Art Festival 2026 programme (Creative Scotland)](https://www.creativescotland.com/news-stories/latest-news/archive/2026/04/edinburgh-art-festival-reveal-2026-programme-across-the-city)
+- [Military Tattoo 2026 first look](https://www.edinburghchamber.co.uk/the-royal-edinburgh-military-tattoo-unveils-a-first-look-at-the-2026-show/)
+- [Edinburgh Deaf Festival 2026 (Creative Scotland)](https://www.creativescotland.com/news-stories/latest-news/archive/2026/07/fifth-edinburgh-deaf-festival---bigger-brighter-bolder-than-ever)

input.body:
Closes #195

Research + proposal only — **no app code changes**.

## What the research found

August is at least **eight overlapping festivals**, not one. Two numbers govern everything:

- **The Fringe is ~80% of August's events** (3,649 shows vs ~900 across the other seven). Anything ranked on relevance or proximity shows a Fringe-only city.
- **Scarcity runs the opposite way.** A Fringe show plays ~25 times; a Book Festival author appears once; an EIFF screening is often a single showing. Volume ranking buries exactly what can't be seen twice.

The data is more available than expected: the **official Edinburgh Festivals Listings API** is free, covers all 11 festivals, and carries venue coordinates, start/end/duration, real prices (which the edfringe GraphQL API does not) and an `is_at_fixed_time` flag that already separates timed events from drop-in exhibitions. Two sharp edges: it has **no availability field at all**, and its licence **bars redistributing dumps to third parties** — which this repo's committed-static-JSON-on-Pages architecture may read as. That's the one genuine blocker, and it's resolvable with one email.

## Wiki changes

- **New `product-wiki/festival-season/`** — the August cluster with dates/scale/venues, the June–July season, the non-festival seasonal city, the six shapes an "event" takes, the locations picture (incl. Fringe by the Sea being 25 miles away), and the full data-availability assessment. All cited; every figure is a published programme claim, none verified against a live API response.
- **`market-and-audience/`** — added "The Fringe is not all of August" under Scale; key insight 1 rewritten from the year-on-year shrink to the cluster.
- **`competitor-landscape/`** — added the cross-festival field: Data Thistle lists ten festivals and plans none; almost every app in the Listings API's gallery is Fringe-only despite the data covering all 11. Key insight 4 goes from two unclaimed claims to three. Evidence weakness recorded rather than claiming the field empty.
- Index README updated.

## The proposal — `docs/multi-festival-design.md`

Written to answer the specific brief that *a film screening must not look like a stand-up show*. The core model is **two independent axes**:

> **Shape decides the silhouette and the logic. Festival decides the colour and the mark.**

Six shapes — run / season / one-off / anchor / drop-in / occasion — derived at normalize time, not fetched. Only `run` is modelled today; `one-off` and `drop-in` break the most assumptions.

**Now page:** a scarcity line (`on again tomorrow` vs `⚡ only tonight`), drop-in exhibitions as the answer to an empty list, a festival filter card, a deliberate cap on consecutive same-festival rows, and no fake sold-out parity for festivals whose source has no availability field.

**Planner** (the intricate half, as expected): a fixed-points band above the run lanes on one shared date axis, one-offs as auto-pinned **anchors** the greedy fills around (the existing pin mechanism is the seam), gap offers for drop-ins instead of scheduling them, out-of-city venues that refuse to estimate travel, and — the biggest single unlock — **scarcity-weighted "Pick my best dates"**: score `1/performances` instead of counting, so a one-off outscores a 25-date Fringe run 25:1. That turns date-picking from "the week with the most stuff" into "the week where the things you can't otherwise see are happening."

The proposal also names what this costs (the product's name, Fringe depth vs city breadth, a permanent availability asymmetry) and the five decisions it can't make itself.

## Verification

- `npm run verify` — green
- Claudinite world + work scopes — clean, with a see-it-fail proving the product-wiki checks actually see the new page

August is **eight overlapping festivals**, and two numbers govern every design decision:

- The Fringe is **~80% of August's events** (3,649 shows vs ~900 across the other seven). Any proximity- or relevance-ranked list shows a Fringe-only city.
- **Scarcity runs the opposite way.** A Fringe show plays ~25 times; a Book Festival author appears once; an EIFF screening is often a single showing. Volume ranking buries exactly what can't be seen twice.

The best find: the **official Edinburgh Festivals Listings API** is free, covers all 11 festivals, and carries venue lat/long, start/end/duration, *real prices* (which the edfringe GraphQL API deliberately doesn't), and an `is_at_fixed_time` flag that already separates timed events from drop-in exhibitions. That's the one genuine blocker, and it's one email to resolve.

## How I answered the "a screening must not look like a stand-up show" brief

Two independent axes, because the two reasons want different mechanisms:

> **Shape decides the silhouette and the logic. Festival decides the colour and the mark.**

Six shapes: **run / season / one-off / anchor / drop-in / occasion**, derived at normalize time rather than fetched. Only `run` is modelled today. A Book Festival one-off and an EIFF screening share a silhouette in different festival colours; a Fringe run and an EIF season share a time-block silhouette but differ in how many dates they offer. That's what stops it collapsing into either eight identical cards in eight paint jobs, or one shape per festival (which breaks the moment EIF programmes an exhibition — and it does).

**Now page:** a scarcity line (`on again tomorrow` vs `⚡ only tonight`), drop-in exhibitions as the answer to the empty list — a drop-in can never fail on timing, only on distance — a festival filter card, and a deliberate cap on consecutive same-festival rows.

**Planner** (much more intricate, as you predicted): a fixed-points band above the run lanes on one shared date axis, one-offs as auto-pinned **anchors** the greedy fills around (your existing pin mechanism is the seam), gap offers for drop-ins instead of scheduling them, and the biggest unlock — **scarcity-weighted "Pick my best dates"**: score `1/performances` instead of counting, so a one-off outscores a 25-date Fringe run 25:1. That changes the question from "which week has the most stuff" to "which week has the things I can't otherwise see."

On your festival-diversity goal specifically: I've written it as an explicit product-values decision rather than burying it as a heuristic, because ranking for diversity means giving up some optimality on purpose. Section 8 lists the five decisions the proposal can't make for you.

Two things I'd flag: every figure is a published programme claim — nobody has registered an API key or made a real call yet — and "EdFringeNow" as a name for eight festivals will get asked about the moment this ships.

Want me to watch the PR for CI and review comments?

input.title: Research Fringe ticketing: who actually sells tickets, the definitive provider list, and listings/affiliate APIs
input.body:
From the owner, in their own words:

> I want you to do more research about how tickets are purchased specifically in the Fringe. I think that edfringe.com and edfest.com are both just fronts for the event organizers themselves, like Assembly, Gilded Balloon, Edinburgh Playhouse, etcetera. Can you get a definitive list of all the event providers in the Fringe? And if you can get the API or whatever guide we need to sell the tickets ourselves instead of edfringe, that would be great. Is there a way to know if we've indeed covered all the event providers? Are there APIs for listings that we can fetch from these event providers and stop scraping edfringe.com?

## Scope

1. **How Fringe ticket sales actually work** — the Fringe Society central box office vs venue-operator box offices, the allocation model, what platform each runs on, and what edfest.com actually is (test the "both are fronts for the organizers" premise).
2. **The definitive provider list** — venue operators of the 2026 Fringe, grounded in the scraped catalogue (the registered programme is the exhaustive universe), with a completeness check: every venue mapped to an operator, unmatched tail listed.
3. **Selling tickets ourselves** — any affiliate, agent, reseller, white-label or API scheme from the Fringe Society, the venue operators, or their ticketing platforms.
4. **Listings APIs** — machine-readable listings from providers or aggregators, and whether any of it could replace scraping edfringe.com.

Research lands in the product wiki; no app code changes.

# Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society: Key Facts

## Legal Status
The Society is both a registered charity and a company limited by guarantee. It was formally incorporated on "22 May 1969...as a company limited by guarantee with a board of directors."

## Governance & Control
The organization has a board of directors overseeing core staff. Membership is open to anyone. The current chair is Benny Higgins (succeeded Timothy O'Shea in 2021). Phoebe Waller-Bridge became the first President in 2021.

## Role & Policy
The Society performs no curatorial function. Instead, it "formalises the process of event registration, promotion and ticket selling, while also acting in an advisory and advocacy capacity." A founding principle: "no single individual or committee should determine who can appear." The Fringe remains "an open access arts festival, accommodating anyone with a desire to perform and a venue willing to host them."

## Box Office & Ticketing
The Society operates the Fringe Shop and box office from its Royal Mile offices (designated "Venue 1"). It provides ticketing services but no information about specific platforms or technology systems appears in this document.

## Relationship to Venues
The Society does not control venues—it coordinates with independent venue operators who choose to participate in the Fringe.

# Red61's Edinburgh Festival Fringe History

## Origins and Timeline
Red61 began powering Fringe ticketing in **2005**, starting with The Famous Spiegeltent at George Square Gardens, which sold 18,000 tickets that first year. Founder Tony Davey had worked at the Fringe since the early 1990s before launching the ticketing service.

## Current Scale
By 2019, the system processed 2.8 million tickets during a single month. Today, Red61's network handles:
- 360 venues
- 600+ performance spaces
- 4,000+ shows daily
- 55,000 performances

As Davey notes: *"During the festival, our ticketing system processes a stadium's worth of tickets every single day."*

## Infrastructure Model
Red61 initially built a physical federated network connecting up to 71 sites across Edinburgh using fiber optic cables and proprietary Redgate Monitor routers, enabling cross-selling between venues. *"Each site had a Redgate Monitor, a proprietary Red61 router, that allowed ticketing servers to talk to each other."*

## Box Office Operations
Red61 ran the Fringe Society box office from 2009 to 2023, managing 90 staff during peak season.

## Current Evolution
By 2025, the infrastructure shifted to cloud-based solutions. *"Everything is in the cloud now – all you need is an internet connection and good Wi-Fi."* After 2023, 95% of tickets became digital, eliminating physical printers and routers.

Your way into the best of the Fringe
EdFest.com is a unique collaboration between some of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe’s leading venues, including Assembly, C ARTS, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Pleasance, Underbelly and ZOO.
Built by the venues that power the Fringe, EdFest brings shows together on a single, cross-venue platform, making it easier for audiences to discover, plan, and book their festival experience.
Audiences can browse comedy, theatre, circus, cabaret, dance, music, and family shows across multiple venues, then book tickets from different venues in a single basket.
EdFest is designed to make booking the Fringe easier, smarter and better value. With booking fees capped at £5 per transaction, audiences can pay less than on other platforms where transaction fees can be as high as £9.
EdFest also gives audiences access to curated offers and exclusive ticket deals that cannot be found elsewhere, helping more people experience more of the Fringe throughout August.
For added peace of mind, customers can choose optional ticket protection through XCover at the point of purchase, helping protect them if they are unable to attend.
Love the Fringe
Love the Fringe is EdFest’s membership scheme, created to help audiences see more shows while supporting the artists, producers and venues that make the festival possible.
Members receive access to free Fringe tickets, exclusive ticket offers, selected discounted tickets and festival bar discounts throughout August.
It is the insider way to experience the Fringe, giving audiences more access, more value and more reasons to discover something new.
For artists and venues, Love the Fringe helps turn available seats into new audiences, stronger word-of-mouth and long-term support for the wider Fringe ecosystem.
Supporting artists, producers and venues
EdFest is more than a ticketing site. It is designed to support the wider Fringe community by giving artists, producers and venues more control over how their shows are presented, promoted and sold.
Participating companies can claim their own show pages, add richer content, run tailored offers and reach new audiences in more flexible ways.
Our aim is simple: to make the Fringe easier to explore, fairer to book and stronger for the people who create it.
EdFest is your way into the best of the Fringe.

## Minimum Allocation Requirement

Every ticketed show must allocate a minimum of 25% of its tickets to the Fringe Box Office.

## How to Allocate Tickets

You will set the number of tickets you wish to offer for sale through the Fringe Box Office on the Payout and Fringe Allocation page in the Show section.

## Commission and Sales Process

An administrative commission of 5% plus VAT is applied on the face value of all tickets sold as part of the payout process. The Fringe Box Office opens earlier than many venue box offices, and because of this many companies allocate half or more of their tickets to our Box Office.

## Allocation of Unsold Tickets

Venues can also allocate additional tickets to the Fringe Box Office at any time, so it's worth checking back now and then to see if a show has available tickets. This allows participants to sell remainder tickets through the Fringe Box Office after the initial allocation.

## Support for Participants

The Artist Services team offers guidance and support around the practicalities of bringing a show to the Fringe, from finding a venue and booking accommodation to immigration guidance, music licensing and much more.

For example, if £100 in membership sales results in a £70 profit after costs, then £35 is allocated to artists and £35 to venues. This equitable model ensures that even free ticket redemptions contribute value to those who create and host performances, supporting a more sustainable approach to discount ticketing.

 Ticket booking

## Developer and 2023 Partnership

Since the start of 2023, the Fringe Society have been working with Australian-based agency equ on developing a new app for this year's festival. equ previously supported Artrage with the development of an app for the Fringe World festival in Perth, Australia.

## Interim Website Partnership

The Edinburgh Fringe chose to work with equ, the developers of the official EdFringe app since 2023 – they were already familiar with the complexities of the Fringe, and easy integration between the website and the app was a bonus. ## App Launch

## Festival Programme

The Dance Base Festival 2026 programme brings together 23 shows from 12 countries to reimagine activism, heritage and identity through the body, in the home of dance at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. The festival features everything from Breakdancing to Butoh, from Pole Dance to politics, with multiple perspectives colliding under one roof.

## Dates

The festival runs from 7-30 August 2026.

## Tickets

Tickets went on sale on Friday at 12 noon at assemblyfestival.com and on Monday 30 March at edfest.com (these dates have already passed since we're in July 2026).

## Additional Information

2026 is a landmark year for Dance Base as the organisation celebrates 25 years in its purpose-built home in the heart of Edinburgh's Grassmarket. Dance Base also hosts a vibrant programme of public and professional dance classes from Monday 3 – Sunday 31 August.

You can access the digital programme and find more details on the Dance Base website (dancebase.co.uk) or through the Assembly Festival ticketing platform.

## Ticketing Allocation Between Fringe Box Office and Venues

Every ticketed show must allocate at least 25% of tickets per performance to the Fringe Box Office. This percentage can be increased when filling in the Show Registration Form, or at any point during the run via the Box Office Reporting Portal.

## Dual Sales Channels

Shows can choose to sell some tickets through the Fringe Box Office and the remainder through the venue – with allocation discussed between the performer and venue manager. Many venues operate an on-site box office as well.

## Fringe Box Office Operations

The Fringe Box Office sells tickets for all shows registered with the Society over the counter, by phone, on edfringe.com and through the Fringe app. Because the Fringe Box Office opens earlier than many venue box offices, many companies allocate half or more of their tickets to the Fringe Box Office.

## Commission

An administrative commission of 5% plus VAT is applied on the face value of all tickets sold through the Fringe Box Office.

findings.fact: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society Limited is a registered Scottish charity (SC002995) and a company limited by guarantee (Companies House SC046605), registered 10 Dec 1968 / incorporated 22 May 1969, with income of £8.28m in FY2024.

The Society is membership-controlled and independent of venue operators: membership costs £5/year and members elect the Board of Directors, adopt accounts and appoint auditors; its constitution bars vetting of the programme (open access — anyone with a desire to perform and a venue willing to host them is in).

The Society 'formalises the process of event registration, promotion and ticket selling' and performs no curatorial function; it publishes the programme, runs the central box office/Fringe Shop (Venue 1) and does not control venues, which are independent operators.

Allocation model (Society's own participant guidance): 'Every ticketed show must allocate a minimum of 25% of its tickets per performance to the Fringe', set on a sliding scale per venue dateline, and 'A 5% (plus VAT) commission from the sale of every ticket sold through the Fringe Box Office is payable to The Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society', with payout by end of September.

The edfringe FAQ describes exactly what NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE means: the Fringe Box Office is allocated a percentage of tickets to sell on behalf of each show; when its allocation is sold, listings advise customers to 'check with the venue box office for further ticket allocation', and venues can top up the Fringe allocation at any time. In the repo's scraped 2026 data this status appears on 1,279 of 59,925 performances (2.1%) across 192 shows, concentrated at Monkey Barrel, Pleasance, Gilded Balloon, theSpace, The Stand, Traverse and Assembly.

Assembly's 2026 performer pack confirms the two-sided model from the venue side: 'Our box office syncs live with that of the Fringe Society so that tickets will always be available across both sales platforms. We use the Red61 ticketing system (also sometimes referred to as VIA) to process all of our tickets... We operate as your ticket agent'; commission is '4% + VAT... on sales made through Assembly & our partner venues' box offices' vs '5% + VAT... through the Fringe Society's box offices'.

Getting into the programme is open-access registration via the Fringe Society with a tiered registration fee (2025/26: £96+VAT for 1-2 performances, £170+VAT for 3-5, £246+VAT early-bird / £328+VAT standard for full runs); big venues like Assembly register their artists with the Society on the artists' behalf.

The Society's consumer ticketing platform changed after 2024: equ (an Australian digital agency, equ.com.au) has built the official EdFringe app since 2023 and, after being told in spring 2024 the old website could not operate beyond the 2024 festival, built the interim edfringe.com that started selling tickets for Fringe 2025 on 12 March 2025; the app accounts for about 30% of all festival ticket purchases.

The 'Tikketr' name is equ's platform branding, evidenced by the official app's Google Play package id com.tikketr.edfringe.prod and the repo's scrape target edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com; Tikketr is barely documented publicly and equ's own case study does not name it.

Red61 states it 'ran the Fringe Society box office from 2009 to 2023' (starting at the Fringe in 2005 with the Famous Spiegeltent) and that in 2024 the Edinburgh Fringe had '17 instances [of Red61] all talking to each other', with the Fringe Society having 'access to all connected instances' — a federated cross-selling network across venue groups that still powers venue box offices (Assembly confirms Red61/VIA for 2026).

A permanent replacement website for edfringe.com is being built by Storm ID under the Society's DCMS/Bloomberg-funded digital transformation strategy, commencing August 2025 and due in time for Fringe 2027 — meaning the current Tikketr/equ site the repo scrapes is explicitly an interim platform.

EdFest.com is operated by Showcatcher Ltd, registered in England and Wales, company number 07628569, registered office Flat 3, 37 Station Road, London SW13 0LF ('References to EdFest... mean Showcatcher Ltd trading as EdFest.com').

Showcatcher Ltd's directors are William Walter Burdett-Coutts (appointed 2011), Daniel Alexander Greenwood and Alexander James Innes (both 2020); Burdett-Coutts is the founder and artistic director of Assembly, and Showcatcher was originally Assembly's digital/streaming platform — so EdFest.com is corporately anchored in Assembly.

EdFest.com describes itself as 'a unique collaboration between some of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe's leading venues' — Assembly, C ARTS, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Pleasance, Underbelly and ZOO (the 2024 site listed eight founders including Summerhall Arts) — initiated in 2022 after the Covid hiatus; it sells only participating venues' Fringe shows (no Tattoo or International Festival), with booking fees capped at £5 per transaction vs 'up to £9' elsewhere.

EdFest.com's selling model is agency, not own inventory: 'As a ticketing platform, EdFest.com acts as an agent on behalf of multiple venues and producers, and we do not hold the rights or inventory to modify tickets'; participating companies 'manage Love the Fringe allocations through their Red61 reporting site', venues receive 50% of booking-fee income, commission was described as 3% (2024) and is 0% for shows allocating at least 4% of inventory to the Love the Fringe membership scheme.

The venue alliance behind EdFest launched its own ticket-selling website ahead of the official programme launch amid open conflict with the Fringe Society (a row over the dropped Fringe app in 2022; Assembly's Burdett-Coutts later said he had 'lost confidence' in the Society and cited 'a serious failure in communication between the Fringe Society and Fringe venues') — direct evidence that the venues do not control edfringe.com.

Other sales channels: venue-operator websites and on-street box offices cross-sell each other's inventory (Assembly tickets are sold in person at Gilded Balloon, Pleasance, Underbelly or any EdFest venue box office and at Edfest.com); the Society runs the physical Fringe Box Office at 180 High Street plus the official app; the Half Price Hut physical structure was retired in 2022 (end of life; formerly Virgin Money-sponsored at The Mound) but half-price offers continue via the Fringe Shop/Box Office and edfringe.com/tickets/half-price-hut, on the Royal Mile again at Fringe 2025.

New for 2026: a West End-style ticket lottery pilot for sold-out Fringe shows via the third-party Sold Out Board website, offering standard-price (not discounted) last tickets for a limited number of sold-out shows.

Face-value resale of at least some Fringe shows happens on Twickets (e.g. an 'Edinburgh Fringe: 5 Headliners' listing), but no evidence of an official Fringe-wide resale partner was found; EdFest's terms ban resale for commercial gain.

Edinburgh Playhouse is owned and operated by ATG (Ambassador Theatre Group), a 3,059-seat touring/receiving house at the top of Leith Walk used for West End tours, EIF and some Fringe events (e.g. ATG's 'Forth on the Fringe', 7 Aug 2026) — it is not a Fringe venue operator like Assembly or Gilded Balloon, and is not part of EdFest; however, it IS a registered Fringe venue in 2026 (venue 59 in the repo's scraped data, hosting Connor Burns, Daniel Sloss, Michelle Wolf and Troy Hawke).

In 2024 (Red61 era) the Fringe Society's central sales operation could sell 'a ticket for every event included in the festival program' by accessing all connected venue instances, and Red61 cross-instance connectivity lets one client's system cross-sell other clients' inventory — the architectural precedent for how EdFest and venue box offices cross-sell today.

keyClaims: edfringe.com is run by the Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society — an independent, membership-governed registered charity and company limited by guarantee that no venue operator owns or controls (they have publicly feuded with it) — and its box office sells each show under an allocation model (minimum 25% of tickets per performance, 5%+VAT commission), with NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE meaning the central allocation is exhausted but the venue's own Red61 box office may still have tickets.

edfest.com, by contrast, really is the major venue operators' own storefront: operated by Showcatcher Ltd (company 07628569, led by Assembly founder William Burdett-Coutts) as a declared ticket agent for seven operators (Assembly, C ARTS, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Pleasance, Underbelly, ZOO) on Red61 rails — so it covers only those venues' shows, never the full ~3,600-show catalogue.

Since March 2025 edfringe.com and the official app run on equ's Tikketr platform (the API the repo scrapes) as an explicitly interim system — Red61 ran the Society's ticketing until 2023/24 and still powers the venue operators' own box offices, and a permanent Storm ID-built site is due for Fringe 2027, meaning the scrape target is likely to change again and remains the only single source covering every registered show.
openQuestions: Exact mechanics of Society-venue inventory sync in the Tikketr era: Assembly says its Red61 box office 'syncs live' with the Fringe Society's platform, while Society guidance describes a sliding-scale allocation with a 25% minimum — whether allocations are now dynamic/continuous or periodically topped up is not published.

The precise cutover year for consumer sales: Red61 says it ran the Fringe Society box office 2009-2023, but the old website (and presumably its Red61 ticketing) operated through the 2024 festival, with the first Tikketr/equ sales on 12 March 2025 — who processed edfringe.com sales during 2024 is not cleanly documented.

Whether the Fringe Society offers any affiliate, agent or API programme for third parties on the Tikketr platform — no public evidence found either way (the Society's arts-industry accreditation ticketing platform exists for industry bookers, but consumer-facing third-party selling terms were not found).
Whether an official Fringe-wide ticket resale channel exists (Twickets carries some Fringe listings; EdFest bans commercial resale; no Society-wide policy or partner found).
The hotel concierge / travel-agent sales channel: no published 2025/2026 source found describing concierge or trade agents selling Fringe tickets.
Why Summerhall Arts appears in the 2024 EdFest founder list of eight venues but not the current seven-venue list — whether its departure was formal was not established.
Storm ID's Fringe-2027 website scope: whether it replaces the Tikketr ticketing engine or only the front-end web experience is not stated in accessible sources.

The precise cutover year for consumer sales: Red61 says it ran the Fringe Society box office 2009-2023, but the old website (and presumably its Red61 ticketing) operated through the 2024 festival, with the first Tikketr/equ sales on 12 March 2025 — who processed edfringe.com sales during 2024 is not cleanly documented.

Whether the Fringe Society offers any affiliate, agent or API programme for third parties on the Tikketr platform — no public evidence found either way (the Society's arts-industry accreditation ticketing platform exists for industry bookers, but consumer-facing third-party selling terms were not found).
Whether an official Fringe-wide ticket resale channel exists (Twickets carries some Fringe listings; EdFest bans commercial resale; no Society-wide policy or partner found).
The hotel concierge / travel-agent sales channel: no published 2025/2026 source found describing concierge or trade agents selling Fringe tickets.
Why Summerhall Arts appears in the 2024 EdFest founder list of eight venues but not the current seven-venue list — whether its departure was formal was not established.
Storm ID's Fringe-2027 website scope: whether it replaces the Tikketr ticketing engine or only the front-end web experience is not stated in accessible sources.

CONTEXT (shared by all researchers):
You are researching for EdFringeNow, a client-side web product for the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (discovery + trip planner). The repo currently gets its show catalogue by scraping edfringe.com's GraphQL API (Tikketr platform, edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com) nightly via GitHub Actions. The owner wants to understand how Fringe tickets are ACTUALLY sold, who all the "event providers" (venue operators) are, whether a third party can sell tickets itself (affiliate/agent/API), and whether provider or aggregator listings APIs could replace the edfringe scrape.

TODAY is 2026-07-31. The 2026 Fringe runs 7-31 August (3,649 shows, 258 venues). Prefer 2025/2026 sources; older sources are fine for structural facts if you say so.

TOOLING CONSTRAINTS: You have WebSearch and WebFetch. edfringe.com returns 403 to WebFetch and equhost.com is blocked by the egress proxy - for those domains rely on WebSearch result snippets and third-party coverage. Most other sites (venue operators, news, wikis) are fetchable; if a fetch fails, fall back to search. Cite EVERY fact with a real URL you actually saw.

OUTPUT: your final output is consumed by a script, not a human. Fill the schema honestly: mark confidence low when a claim rests on one thin source; put what you could NOT establish into openQuestions rather than guessing. keyClaims = the 2-3 claims your topic's conclusions rest on (the ones that, if wrong, change the product decision).

1. PBH's Free Fringe: how it works (unticketed, pass-the-bucket, no advance tickets?), where its listings live (own site/wee book?), scale in 2025/2026.
2. Laughing Horse Free Festival: same questions; do they do any advance/reserved tickets (e.g. via Eventbrite or their own site)?
3. Other mid-tier / independent operators active in 2025-2026: Sweet Venues, Paradise Green, Bedlam Theatre, Army @ The Fringe, Hill Street / Institut francais d'Ecosse, Quaker Meeting House, French Institute, Riddle's Court, any others you find. One line + citation each; skip any you cannot confirm for 2025/2026.
4. THE COMPLETENESS QUESTION: the Fringe is open-access - every show must register with the Fringe Society to be "in the Fringe", so the official programme/venue directory is by construction the exhaustive universe of providers. Confirm this open-access registration fact with citations (Fringe Society "how to take part" / venue registration guidance via search snippets). Is there a published venue directory or venue association (e.g. the Fringe Society's venue list, any "association of independent venues") a third party can enumerate?
5. Do free shows appear in edfringe.com's data like any other show (our scrape shows FREE_NON_TICKETED / FREE_TICKETED statuses - consistent with that)?

Based on the search results, here's how PBH's Free Fringe works:

## How It Works

PBH's Free Fringe, founded by Peter Buckley Hill, runs a notable number of venues around the city in August. There is no venue hire charge and free entrance for everyone. If the audience like the show, they put a voluntary donation in a bucket at the end.

## No Advance Tickets Required

content.content:
# Laughing Horse Free Festival: Entry & Ticketing Overview

## Entry Model
The Free Festival operates primarily on a **free entry with voluntary contributions** system. Audiences aren't charged admission; instead, they're asked to contribute "on the way out" through collections.

## Pay What You Can Option
Yes, a Pay What You Can ticketing system exists with advance reservations. The site notes: *"audiences aren't charged to come in...for some shows have the option to get a 'Pay What You Can' ticket in advance, all of which goes 100% to the performer."*

Average donations for standard free shows range from £2-£3, while Pay What You Can shows with advance reservations average £6-£8.

## Ticketing Platform
The content indicates Main Fringe programme entry is required (approximately £295 for full runs), suggesting use of the official **Edinburgh Fringe database/programme** rather than independent ticketing platforms like Eventbrite.

## Venues & Spaces
The Free Festival operates **25+ venues** with over **38 performance spaces** (as of 2019 data). Notable mega-venues include:
- The Three Sisters
- The Counting House (ballroom)
- Cabaret Voltaire

Venue capacities range from 20 to 150 attendees.

# Laughing Horse Free Festival: Entry & Ticketing Overview

## Entry Model
The Free Festival operates primarily on a **free entry with voluntary contributions** system. Audiences aren't charged admission; instead, they're asked to contribute "on the way out" through collections.

## Pay What You Can Option
Yes, a Pay What You Can ticketing system exists with advance reservations. The site notes: *"audiences aren't charged to come in...for some shows have the option to get a 'Pay What You Can' ticket in advance, all of which goes 100% to the performer."*

Average donations for standard free shows range from £2-£3, while Pay What You Can shows with advance reservations average £6-£8.

## Ticketing Platform
The content indicates Main Fringe programme entry is required (approximately £295 for full runs), suggesting use of the official **Edinburgh Fringe database/programme** rather than independent ticketing platforms like Eventbrite.

## Venues & Spaces
The Free Festival operates **25+ venues** with over **38 performance spaces** (as of 2019 data). Notable mega-venues include:
- The Three Sisters
- The Counting House (ballroom)
- Cabaret Voltaire

Venue capacities range from 20 to 150 attendees.

# PBH's Free Fringe: Entry, Donations, and Ticketing Rules

## Free Entry Requirement

PBH's Free Fringe **does forbid charging admission**. The foundational principle states: *"The shows are free to the public to attend"* and *"It's free."* Shows cannot charge ticket prices for entry.

## Donations and Collections

Rather than paid admission, performers use voluntary audience donations. The guidelines note: *"Most performers make a 'bucket speech' at the end of the show to accept donations from the audience."*

Critically, the organization emphasizes respectful fundraising: *"It is totally against the ethos of the Free Fringe to be rude to people who do not donate."*

## Ticketing Restrictions

Performers cannot simultaneously operate shows with other "free" organizations that use pay-for-priority models. The rule specifies applicants *"must not have a current application (this year) for a FREE ADMISSION show with any other organisation"* including Laughing Horse and similar venues.

However, performers **may** do fully ticketed shows at paid venues during the same Fringe season, as the restrictions apply only to competing free-admission organizations.

## Venue Revenue Model

Venues benefit indirectly: *"the venues benefit from the money spent at their bars and counters"* rather than through ticket sales or performer fees.

## Overview
Paradise Green is at the heart and soul of the largest arts festival in the world, presenting a wide range of top-quality performances. Paradise Green is a volunteer-run, not-for-profit organisation which runs venues at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe each summer.

## Venues
Paradise Green has five diverse performance spaces across two wonderful venues: Paradise in Augustines and Paradise in the Vault.

### Paradise in Augustines
Paradise in Augustines is a church during the rest of the year and is converted for the festival period. It houses two largest spaces in addition to the newest intimate space: The Snug.

The three spaces at Paradise in Augustines are:
- The Sanctuary seats 110 and is the largest performance space.
- The Studio seats up to 107 depending on chosen layout.
- The Snug is the new intimate performance space with 30 seats.

### Paradise in the Vault
Paradise in The Vault has a purpose built small-scale theatre space set in the vaulted basement of the building as the main performance area, and a second space that is converted anew each year. This venue tends to cater for smaller scale and more experimental productions.

Bedlam Theatre is uniquely located in a converted neo-gothic church at the heart of the Fringe and is the year-round home of the Edinburgh University Theatre Company.

Bedlam Theatre (Venue 49) is a student-run theatre inside a former Gothic church dating from 1848, seating around 90. The theatre is located at 11b Bristo Pl.

Pleasance operates three Edinburgh sites in 2026 (Pleasance Courtyard, Pleasance Dome, Pleasance at EICC) with on-site box offices, and pleasance.co.uk sells Fringe tickets directly: show pages link to booking paths of the form /via/tickets/33%3A301593 — Red61 VIA embedded in their own domain

Gilded Balloon runs four 2026 venues (Teviot Row House, Patter House, Gilded Balloon at the Museum, new Gilded Saloon) with 200+ shows, selling direct at tickets.gildedballoon.co.uk which advertises 'exclusive discounts and low booking fees when booking direct'; that site runs the Red61 WordPress theme (/wp-content/themes/red61/) with VIA event IDs (/event/14:6104)

Summerhall Arts presents 72 shows plus 9 in a new Sauna Theatre for Fringe 2026 (6-31 Aug) via festival.summerhallarts.co.uk; its ticket site tickets.summerhallarts.co.uk is a Red61 white-label served from summerhallarts.online.red61.co.uk

Summerhall's published 2025 Festival Information Pack states: 'The EdFringe Box Office Commission is 5%, and the Summerhall Arts Box Office Commission is 8% [4% on the Box Office Split deal]. Summerhall's pack also describes the conventional venue deal (60% of box office income to the show / 40% to the venue, versus a minimum guarantee) and says the venue's box office system 'is linked to the Fringe box office', with EdFringe and venue receipts totalled together at settlement

ZOO returns for its 25th Fringe in 2026 with three sites (ZOO Southside, ZOO Charteris, High School Yards) and sells directly at tickets.zoofestival.co.uk with VIA event IDs (/event/124:1938) and Red61 markers in the page; Red61's own 20-years article names ZOO as a user of its Front of House app

C ARTS / C venues runs hub venues C primo (Hill Street) and C royale (Royal Society of Edinburgh, George Street) plus the C digital online venue; its booking site CtheArts.com (res.cthearts.com) is a Red61 white-label (wp-content/themes/red61, /event/34:3397 VIA IDs) charging £1.00/ticket handling capped at £6/transaction

C ARTS' how-to-book page documents venue-to-venue cross-selling: 'Tickets for all C venues shows are also available from www.edfest.com and from our cross-selling partner venues Assembly, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Paradise Green, Pleasance, Summerhall, Underbelly, and Zoo. The C ARTS box office also sells tickets for shows at these venues'

theSpaceUK operates an 11-space hub at Surgeons Quarter plus 8 theatres on the Royal Mile for 2026 (199 new shows announced) and for 2026 sells through its own site and an on-site box office; tickets.thespaceuk.com ('theSpaceUK Official Tickets') is a Red61 white-label (wp-content/themes/red61, uploads/sites/88, event IDs like 911:3690)

Greenside operates two 2026 hubs — Greenside @ George Street (7 studios, Royal Society of Edinburgh building) and Greenside @ Riddles Court (4 studios) plus the GreenScreen online venue; its GoDaddy-built site greensidevenue.co.uk has no online box office, and its shows are bookable through edfringe.com — effectively 'sells only via edfringe'

Just the Tonic runs multiple 2026 sites (Legends on Cowgate, The Mash House, Nucleus, The Caves, The Hive — c.15+ rooms) with box office 0330 220 1212; its ticket site edinburgh.justthetonic.com runs the Red61 WordPress theme, i.e. Red61 VIA white-label

Monkey Barrel Comedy hosts 150+ shows over eight venues at Fringe 2026; its announcements direct Fringe bookings to the Edinburgh Fringe website, while its own year-round/preview sales run at booking.monkeybarrelcomedy.com on the Line-Up platform (liveit.io events and 'liveit' markers in the booking pages)

The Stand Comedy Club sells its Fringe 2026 programme on its own site at thestand.co.uk/fringe-2026 (performance URLs like /performance/22409/...); no third-party platform markers appear in the site, indicating an in-house/unidentified ticketing system; at Fringe time it operates its York Place club plus The Stand's New Town Theatre (Fringe venue number 7)

Traverse Theatre's TravFest26 runs 31 Jul - 30 Aug 2026 with three newly commissioned productions across its two in-house performance spaces plus external venues; traverse.co.uk sells tickets itself and its whats-on pages contain Spektrix integration markers — Traverse runs on Spektrix, not Red61

Dance Base presents its 25th festival programme (23 shows from 12 countries, 7-30 Aug 2026) 'in partnership with Assembly Festival' (listed on edfringe as 'Assembly @ Dance Base'); tickets went on sale at assemblyfestival.com and edfest.com rather than through an independent Dance Base channel

Scottish Storytelling Centre (Netherbow Theatre + Storytelling Court, Royal Mile) runs a curated Fringe 2026 programme and sells tickets online, by phone and in person; its events links point to scottishstorytellingcentre.online.red61.co.uk/events?s=Fringe — a Red61 white-label store

Fringe Society rules require every ticketed show to allocate a minimum of 25% of its tickets per performance to the Fringe Box Office (adjustable upward via a sliding scale and the Box Office Reporting Portal), and 'a 5% (plus VAT) commission from the sale of every ticket sold through the Fringe Box Office is payable to The Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society'

Red61 (Edinburgh-based maker of the VIA ticketing system) has operated at the Fringe since 2005, built a physical cross-selling network of up to 71 sites with 21 servers so venue ticketing servers could talk to each other, and in 2024 ran 17 interconnected Fringe instances 'allowing different groups of venues to work together'

The 'Edinburgh Comedy Festival' was a joint marketing brand of the Big Four venues (Assembly, Gilded Balloon, Pleasance, Underbelly) operated only in August 2008 and 2009, with a joint brochure covering almost 90% of Fringe comedy in 2008; the designation was quietly dropped after widespread media and industry criticism

The 'Big Four' term survives as an informal grouping of Pleasance, Gilded Balloon, Underbelly and Assembly with no current joint sales brand found; William Burdett-Coutts, who founded Assembly in 1981, remains Assembly's Artistic Director for 2026

Edinburgh Playhouse (ATG-operated: access contact edinburghaccess@atgentertainment.com; ATG box office atgtickets.com) IS a registered Fringe venue in 2026 — venue number 59 on edfringe.com — but only for four big comedy one-nighter runs: Daniel Sloss BITTER (14-15 Aug), Troy Hawke (21 Aug), Connor Burns FLOW (22-23 Aug), Michelle Wolf (24 Aug)

'Forth on the Fringe' (7-8 Aug 2026, Forth 1 radio gala at the Playhouse) is sold by ATG Tickets and does not appear among the Playhouse's edfringe.com-listed events, i.e. Playhouse hosts both Fringe-registered and non-Fringe August events side by side

Venue operators actively push direct booking against edfringe.com on price: Gilded Balloon offers 'exclusive discounts and low booking fees when booking direct' plus £7.25 locals' tickets for 141 shows, and C ARTS says 'Tickets are also available from the Fringe website, but for lowest handling fees book here at www.CtheArts.com'

Because the Fringe Box Office opens earlier than many venue box offices, many companies allocate half or more of their tickets to the Fringe Box Office; shows split remaining inventory with the venue by agreement between performer and venue manager

keyClaims: The big commercial Fringe operators all sell the same shows on their own box-office sites in parallel with edfringe.com, and at least 10 of the 15 major operators (Assembly, Pleasance, Underbelly, Gilded Balloon, Summerhall, ZOO, C ARTS, theSpaceUK, Just the Tonic, Scottish Storytelling Centre) run those channels on a single shared platform: Red61 VIA, mostly as *.online.red61.co.uk white-labels with N:XXXX composite event IDs.

Parallel selling is governed by a published Fringe Society rule — a minimum 25% of each performance's tickets must be allocated to the Fringe Box Office (5%+VAT commission) — and Summerhall's published pack quantifies the real-world split at typically 70% edfringe / 30% venue box office, meaning edfringe.com is the majority sales channel and the only complete catalogue.

The exceptions are few and identifiable — Traverse (Spektrix), The Stand (in-house), Monkey Barrel (Line-Up/liveit.io, Fringe runs via edfringe), Greenside (edfringe-only), Dance Base (via Assembly) — so venue/provider APIs alone can never cover the full show catalogue, and any provider-side data or affiliate strategy is essentially a question about access to Red61 VIA.
openQuestions: Whether Red61 offers a public or partner-facing listings/affiliate API that a third party like EdFringeNow could use (Eventotron integrates with Red61 for participants, but consumer-side API access terms were not established).

How venue Red61 inventories sync with edfringe.com's Tikketr platform since the Fringe Society changed systems — Summerhall says its box office is 'linked to the Fringe box office', but the mechanism, latency and whether allocations are live-shared post-Tikketr is unverified.
The Stand's underlying ticketing software vendor (no third-party markers found; assumed in-house but unconfirmed).
Whether Monkey Barrel sells any full-Fringe-run tickets (not just previews/year-round shows) through its own Line-Up-powered booking site.
Exact per-operator space counts (marketing copy varies; e.g. Assembly's total space count across its 7 hubs and Pleasance's ~25+ spaces were not pinned to a single authoritative 2026 number).

Whether edfest.com (named by both C ARTS and Dance Base as a sales channel) is an independent agent or an Assembly-operated storefront, and what its relationship to the Red61 cross-selling network is.
Whether any formal joint marketing between the Big Four exists today beyond the informal label (nothing found after the 2008-09 Edinburgh Comedy Festival).

The 'Big Four' term survives as an informal grouping of Pleasance, Gilded Balloon, Underbelly and Assembly with no current joint sales brand found; William Burdett-Coutts, who founded Assembly in 1981, remains Assembly's Artistic Director for 2026

Edinburgh Playhouse (ATG-operated: access contact edinburghaccess@atgentertainment.com; ATG box office atgtickets.com) IS a registered Fringe venue in 2026 — venue number 59 on edfringe.com — but only for four big comedy one-nighter runs: Daniel Sloss BITTER (14-15 Aug), Troy Hawke (21 Aug), Connor Burns FLOW (22-23 Aug), Michelle Wolf (24 Aug)

'Forth on the Fringe' (7-8 Aug 2026, Forth 1 radio gala at the Playhouse) is sold by ATG Tickets and does not appear among the Playhouse's edfringe.com-listed events, i.e. Playhouse hosts both Fringe-registered and non-Fringe August events side by side

Venue operators actively push direct booking against edfringe.com on price: Gilded Balloon offers 'exclusive discounts and low booking fees when booking direct' plus £7.25 locals' tickets for 141 shows, and C ARTS says 'Tickets are also available from the Fringe website, but for lowest handling fees book here at www.CtheArts.com'

Because the Fringe Box Office opens earlier than many venue box offices, many companies allocate half or more of their tickets to the Fringe Box Office; shows split remaining inventory with the venue by agreement between performer and venue manager

keyClaims: The big commercial Fringe operators all sell the same shows on their own box-office sites in parallel with edfringe.com, and at least 10 of the 15 major operators (Assembly, Pleasance, Underbelly, Gilded Balloon, Summerhall, ZOO, C ARTS, theSpaceUK, Just the Tonic, Scottish Storytelling Centre) run those channels on a single shared platform: Red61 VIA, mostly as *.online.red61.co.uk white-labels with N:XXXX composite event IDs.

Parallel selling is governed by a published Fringe Society rule — a minimum 25% of each performance's tickets must be allocated to the Fringe Box Office (5%+VAT commission) — and Summerhall's published pack quantifies the real-world split at typically 70% edfringe / 30% venue box office, meaning edfringe.com is the majority sales channel and the only complete catalogue.

The exceptions are few and identifiable — Traverse (Spektrix), The Stand (in-house), Monkey Barrel (Line-Up/liveit.io, Fringe runs via edfringe), Greenside (edfringe-only), Dance Base (via Assembly) — so venue/provider APIs alone can never cover the full show catalogue, and any provider-side data or affiliate strategy is essentially a question about access to Red61 VIA.
openQuestions: Whether Red61 offers a public or partner-facing listings/affiliate API that a third party like EdFringeNow could use (Eventotron integrates with Red61 for participants, but consumer-side API access terms were not established).

How venue Red61 inventories sync with edfringe.com's Tikketr platform since the Fringe Society changed systems — Summerhall says its box office is 'linked to the Fringe box office', but the mechanism, latency and whether allocations are live-shared post-Tikketr is unverified.
The Stand's underlying ticketing software vendor (no third-party markers found; assumed in-house but unconfirmed).
Whether Monkey Barrel sells any full-Fringe-run tickets (not just previews/year-round shows) through its own Line-Up-powered booking site.
Exact per-operator space counts (marketing copy varies; e.g. Assembly's total space count across its 7 hubs and Pleasance's ~25+ spaces were not pinned to a single authoritative 2026 number).

Whether edfest.com (named by both C ARTS and Dance Base as a sales channel) is an independent agent or an Assembly-operated storefront, and what its relationship to the Red61 cross-selling network is.
Whether any formal joint marketing between the Big Four exists today beyond the informal label (nothing found after the 2008-09 Edinburgh Comedy Festival).

CONTEXT (shared by all researchers):
You are researching for EdFringeNow, a client-side web product for the Edinburgh Festival Fringe (discovery + trip planner). The repo currently gets its show catalogue by scraping edfringe.com's GraphQL API (Tikketr platform, edfringe-tikketr-web-api.equhost.com) nightly via GitHub Actions. The owner wants to understand how Fringe tickets are ACTUALLY sold, who all the "event providers" (venue operators) are, whether a third party can sell tickets itself (affiliate/agent/API), and whether provider or aggregator listings APIs could replace the edfringe scrape.

TODAY is 2026-07-31. The 2026 Fringe runs 7-31 August (3,649 shows, 258 venues). Prefer 2025/2026 sources; older sources are fine for structural facts if you say so.

TOOLING CONSTRAINTS: You have WebSearch and WebFetch. edfringe.com returns 403 to WebFetch and equhost.com is blocked by the egress proxy - for those domains rely on WebSearch result snippets and third-party coverage. Most other sites (venue operators, news, wikis) are fetchable; if a fetch fails, fall back to search. Cite EVERY fact with a real URL you actually saw.

OUTPUT: your final output is consumed by a script, not a human. Fill the schema honestly: mark confidence low when a claim rests on one thin source; put what you could NOT establish into openQuestions rather than guessing. keyClaims = the 2-3 claims your topic's conclusions rest on (the ones that, if wrong, change the product decision).

TOPIC: Can a third party SELL Fringe tickets itself - affiliate, agent, reseller, white-label, or ticketing API?

Questions, each cited; for each scheme found record: who offers it, what you get (deep links with commission? an actual purchase API? white-label storefront?), how to apply, cost/commission if published:
1. Does the Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society offer ANY of: an affiliate scheme, a ticket-agent programme, a white-label box office, a public ticketing/purchase API? Search hard: "edfringe affiliate", "fringe society ticket agents", "edfringe API", "fringe box office partner", artist/participant services pages, and their published ticketing terms & conditions. Also: do their T&Cs PROHIBIT unauthorized resale of Fringe tickets?
2. Do the big venue operators (Assembly, Pleasance, Underbelly, Gilded Balloon, Summerhall, Monkey Barrel, The Stand) run affiliate/agent programmes for their own box offices?
3. The ticketing PLATFORMS behind the box offices: Tikketr (equ), Red61 VIA, Spektrix, Citizen Ticket, TicketCo, Ticketsolve. Which of these offer partner/agent/affiliate APIs that would let a licensed third party sell a client's inventory? (Spektrix has a public API for a venue's own integrations; Red61 VIA has agent/API capabilities - verify and characterize.) The point: even where tech exists, does it require a COMMERCIAL AGREEMENT with each operator?
4. Are there existing third-party resellers/agents of Fringe tickets (TodayTix? Fever? hotel concierge programmes? edfest.com itself?) - evidence of what arrangement they have.
5. Realistic bottom line for a small independent site: what would "selling tickets ourselves" actually require, and what is the practical alternative (deep links to each seller, possibly with affiliate commission where schemes exist)?

# PBH's Free Fringe: Overview

## Founding
Peter Buckley Hill established the Free Fringe in 1996 after losing £4,000 as a performer at the 1994 Fringe. He launched it with his show "Peter Buckley Hill And Some Comedians," initially operating from a single venue called Footlights and Firkin.

## Business Model
The Free Fringe operates on a distinctive approach: performers receive free venue access without advance booking fees, provided they don't charge admission. Instead, audiences make voluntary donations after shows. As described, this model "does not charge performers for use of performance spaces, on the condition that they do not charge an entry fee."

## Scale & Growth
The organization expanded dramatically:
- **2009**: 176 shows across 19 venues
- **2015**: 529 free shows on 59 stages, representing over 9,260 performances

## Recognition
The model was "cited as an important development in the Fringe's culture and infrastructure" and credited with restoring the "idealistic spirit of the Fringe." Peter Buckley Hill received the Edinburgh Comedy Awards Panel Prize in 2009 for this work.

## Current Status
Buckley Hill stepped down from managing the festival in 2016. The webpage doesn't mention the Wee Blue Book or edfringe.com registration details.

# Edinburgh Festivals Listings API - Summary

**Approval Process:**
Developers must build applications using a demonstration dataset (`demofringe`) and submit for review before accessing live Fringe data. The review ensures compliance with licence terms and appropriate data presentation.

**Data Provided:**
Event listings including pricing, concession information, and website links for ticketing.

**Licence Terms - Key Restrictions:**

*Linking:* "you must only use the links to edfringe.com provided by the API and must not link to any other ticketing site"

*Ticketing:* Applications should display basic `price` and `concession` data, using the API's `website` parameter to direct users to full ticketing details on the Fringe website.

*Data Freshness:* "you should retrieve fresh data from the API at least every 24 hours"

*Genre Representation:* The Fringe discourages apps covering individual genres alone, promoting diversity.

**Ticket Purchase Capability:**
No direct purchasing through the API; the system only provides links to the Fringe website.

**Operator:**
Managed by inGenerator; operated by Festivals Edinburgh Limited (registered company SC331673).

**Current Status:**
Yes, the page indicates active operations with regular data updates and an ongoing approval workflow.

# Fringe Ticket Sales & Allocation Summary

## Ticket Allocation Requirements
Shows must allocate a minimum of 25% of tickets per performance to the Fringe Box Office. Organizers use a sliding scale to select their preferred allocation percentage above this minimum threshold.

## Payout Structure
Revenue from ticket sales flows through the Fringe Box Office. Organizers choose between two payout options:
- **To their organization**: Funds go to bank details registered on the organization's Payout Details page
- **To the venue's organization**: Funds go to the venue operator

As stated: *"the payout will go to the bank details that you specified on the Payout Details page"* when selecting the first option.

## Commission & Fees
The Fringe Society charges *"a 5% (plus VAT) commission from the sale of every ticket sold through the Fringe Box Office."* No surcharge applies to free shows.

## Payout Timing
*"Payout is processed no later than the end of September after any given Fringe."*

## Access & Control
Only organization administrators and those granted show admin permissions can modify payout specifications. Read-only permission holders can view but not amend these details.

# Edinburgh Festivals Listings API: Licence Summary

## What You CAN Do

**Commercial use is permitted.** The licence states you may "produce works using or incorporating the listings data for any lawful purpose, including commercial applications" and "modify, transform and build upon the listings data."

## What You CANNOT Do

**Ticketing restrictions:** Non-Fringe events can only link to official festival websites, venue sites, or edinburghfestivalcity.com. For Fringe shows specifically, "Links relating to Fringe shows or events must not be made to any other ticketing site, including the venue's own site"—they must point to edfringe.com.

**Data redistribution:** Type A users especially "must not redistribute listings to third parties by means of either data feeds or data dumps." Type C developers face the same restriction.

**Attribution requirements:** Type A and C users must credit the API. Type B (media) users should provide "reasonable attribution...where it is reasonably practical."

## Key Disclaimers

The provider makes no guarantees: "We do not contract to make it available now or at any time or to provide any particular level of service and we reserve the right to suspend the availability of the API at any time." They exclude liability for indirect damages and "loss of profit, opportunity or data."

## Revocation

The provider may terminate if they "reasonably believe that you have failed to comply with any terms." Upon termination, users "must delete all listings data that is under your control."
